strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an important, under-modeled problem: heterogeneity in judge reliability in the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and its consequences for biased rankings and invalid uncertainty quantification.

Clean and rigorous statistical formulation: a judge-aware BTL model with a discrimination-type reliability parameter, with formal identifiability results (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3) and asymptotic theory (consistency and asymptotic normality, Theorem 3.4) that support principled confidence intervals for score differences and rankings.

Simulation studies convincingly validate the theoretical claims: MSE decays at the predicted O(1/T) rate, and the judge-aware model achieves near-nominal coverage while the unweighted BTL model shows systematic and worsening under-coverage as T grows, illustrating the 'confidently wrong' phenomenon motivating the paper.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across multiple real datasets (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a new in-house 45-model dataset), with face-validity checks (e.g., correct GPT-4/Claude ordering, Vicuna-13B > Vicuna-7B, agreement with published MT-Bench rankings) and quantitative comparison to human-derived Chatbot Arena rankings (Spearman correlation improvement).

Practical, implementable estimation procedure (aggregated likelihood, Adam-based optimization with normalization constraints) with reported efficiency gains (narrower CIs, higher data efficiency) over the unweighted baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea (judge/annotator-specific discrimination parameters analogous to 2PL IRT models) closely parallels Otani et al. (2016) and existing BTL asymptotic theory (e.g., Gao et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2024b), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is technically new beyond extending this design to a fully randomized, reference-free judge panel.

The efficiency evaluation in Section 5.3 is partly circular: the 'ground truth' used to assess subsampling efficiency is the full-data fit of the same (weighted or unweighted) model, not an independent gold standard, so the reported efficiency gains partly reflect self-consistency of each method with itself rather than closeness to true model quality.

No empirical comparison to existing LLM-ranking baselines discussed in related work (REM, GTR/FTR, Product-of-Experts), despite these being explicitly positioned as competitors; only the unweighted BTL model is used as a baseline throughout.

The i.i.d. uniform random design assumption underlying the asymptotic theory is unlikely to hold for the real datasets (comparisons are typically unbalanced across pairs/judges), and the paper does not discuss or empirically assess robustness of the inferential guarantees to this mismatch.
Tie handling (encoding ties as y=0.5) is ad hoc and not derived from the probabilistic model, potentially biasing the likelihood in datasets with many ties (mentioned as present in real datasets).

Judge reliability is assumed static across all comparisons/tasks; the exclusion of a judge with γ̂≈0 due to numerical instability suggests potential fragility of the estimator in edge cases that is not deeply investigated.

Human-preference validation is somewhat limited: a single Spearman correlation comparison on Chatbot Arena (0.9955 vs 0.9699) without confidence intervals, significance testing, or broader replication across datasets to substantiate the claimed improvement in alignment with human preference.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a logical progression from model formulation to theory to simulation to real-data experiments.

The core idea—adding a judge-specific discrimination parameter to the BTL model—is a sensible and interpretable way to model judge reliability, and the authors provide formal identifiability, consistency, and asymptotic normality results that enable principled confidence intervals, which is a genuine (if modest) theoretical contribution.

The simulation study in Section 4 convincingly validates the O(1/T) convergence rate and demonstrates the coverage failure of the unweighted BTL model, illustrating the 'confidently wrong' phenomenon the paper emphasizes.

The real-data case studies (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, in-house panel) are diverse and provide some face-validity checks (e.g., recovering known model orderings, higher Spearman correlation with human-preference BTL rankings).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the paper itself cites Otani et al. (2016) as already introducing judge-specific discrimination parameters in an IRT-style pairwise aggregation model, and the proposed model is essentially the free-reference, fully randomized extension of that idea. The asymptotic theory, while a nice addition, is a fairly standard MLE argument for a well-specified parametric model and does not represent a major methodological leap.

Despite extensively reviewing REM, GTR, FTR, Crowd-BT, and Product-of-Experts aggregation as directly competing judge-heterogeneity methods, the paper never empirically compares against any of them. All experiments only contrast the proposed weighted model against a plain unweighted BTL baseline, which is the weakest possible comparator and does not establish that the method outperforms existing alternatives designed for the same problem.

The efficiency experiment in Section 5.3 defines 'ground truth' as the model's own full-data fit (ŝ_ref_w, ŝ_ref_u), making the evaluation partly circular: the weighted model's subsampled estimates are compared to the weighted model's full-data estimate, which trivially favors internal consistency rather than demonstrating external validity.

In the MT-Bench comparison (Table 1), both the weighted and unweighted fits produce the identical ranking, so this experiment does not actually demonstrate any benefit of judge-aware weighting; it is presented as supportive evidence but is largely uninformative for distinguishing the two methods.

The model only captures judges' sensitivity/precision (a symmetric noise-like parameter) and cannot represent systematic directional biases such as self-preference or verbosity bias, which are well-documented and arguably more consequential failure modes of LLM judges; this limitation is not discussed.

Several reported gains are numerically small or of unclear statistical/practical significance (e.g., CI width reductions of 5.4%–13.5%, Spearman correlation 0.9955 vs 0.9699), and Table 2 shows many adjacent-ranked models with overlapping confidence intervals, undermining the claim of meaningfully improved rankings without further discussion of multiple-comparison or practical significance.

Ad hoc exclusion of a judge with γ̂≈0 'due to numerical instability' is not adequately justified or analyzed; this could mask fragility of the estimator in realistic panels where some judges are genuinely near-uninformative, which is precisely the regime the method is meant to handle robustly.

The newly collected in-house dataset lacks sufficient detail in the main text (judge selection, prompt design, potential contamination) to assess reliability of the key efficiency results, and two originally planned judges were dropped due to API issues, raising reproducibility concerns.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: judge heterogeneity in LLM-as-a-judge pipelines is an important, under-modeled issue with real practical consequences (biased leaderboards, invalid uncertainty).

The proposed extension of BTL with judge-specific discrimination parameters is simple, interpretable, and naturally connects to IRT-style discrimination models, with a clean probabilistic interpretation (as opposed to heuristic weighting schemes like FTR).

Solid theoretical contribution: identifiability up to natural normalization (Theorem 3.2/Corollary 3.3) and consistency/asymptotic normality of the MLE (Theorem 3.4), which support principled confidence intervals for score differences and rankings—something existing heuristic LLM-ranking methods (REM, GTR/FTR) lack.

Simulation studies carefully validate the theoretical claims: the O(1/T) convergence rate is empirically confirmed, and coverage/width experiments convincingly show that ignoring judge heterogeneity produces under-coverage that worsens with more data (the 'confidently wrong' phenomenon highlighted in the abstract), while the judge-aware model maintains near-nominal coverage with shorter intervals.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across multiple real datasets (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a new in-house 45-model/18-judge dataset), showing consistent qualitative improvements (e.g., correcting the GPT-4 ranking order relative to Claude variants, preserving known sub-family orderings such as Vicuna-13B > Vicuna-7B) and higher Spearman correlation with human preference rankings (0.9955 vs 0.9699).
Writing and organization are clear, with explicit statements of assumptions, theorems, and a logical flow from theory to simulation to real-data validation.
weaknesses: No empirical comparison against the main competing methods discussed in related work (REM, GTR/FTR, Crowd-BT, Product-of-Experts aggregation); the only empirical comparison is against an unweighted BTL baseline, which likely understates the paper's actual contribution relative to prior work and leaves open whether the gains are specific to naive aggregation rather than to more sophisticated heuristic competitors.

The simulation-based coverage/consistency validation is performed under a correctly-specified data-generating process (data simulated from the same judge-aware BTL model), so it mainly confirms internal theoretical correctness rather than robustness to real-world model misspecification (e.g., judges with non-monotonic or context-dependent biases, non-transitive preferences, prompt-order effects).

Several real-data validations risk circularity: e.g., comparing fitted scores against MT-Bench's own GPT-4-judged scores, or against UltraFeedback preference ratings that may itself derive from similar LLM-judge pipelines, which weakens the independence of the validation signal from the method's own assumptions.

The model assumes a single static scalar reliability γk per judge; reliability is well known to vary by task/domain/prompt difficulty, and this limitation (acknowledged as future work) substantially restricts applicability to realistic heterogeneous evaluation settings where a judge may be reliable on some prompts and unreliable on others.

Handling of ties via y=0.5 is introduced ad hoc and is not clearly reconciled with the Bernoulli likelihood underlying the asymptotic theory; the paper does not discuss how this affects the validity of the stated consistency/normality guarantees in the presence of ties.

Details needed for reproducibility (e.g., exact judge panel composition/prompts, code/data release, full identity of the 45 in-house models and prompts) are deferred to appendices not included here, and there is no explicit reproducibility or ethics statement in the main text.

Scalability and computational cost of the joint MLE optimization (especially for large N, K, T as in real leaderboard-scale settings with hundreds of models) is not discussed, leaving open questions about practical deployment at scale.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical treatment: the paper proves identifiability (up to a natural scale/location normalization), consistency, and asymptotic normality of the MLE for the judge-aware BTL model, with detailed, largely self-contained proofs in the appendix (Fisher information invertibility via a weighted Gram-matrix argument, uniform LLN arguments, Delta method transfer from the free parameterization back to (s, gamma)).

Comprehensive empirical validation spanning simulations (confirming O(1/T) convergence and calibrated coverage vs. under-coverage of the unweighted BTL baseline) and four real-world benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a newly collected 45-model/18-judge dataset), with consistent qualitative conclusions across all of them.

The Chatbot Arena case study is a compelling demonstration: the weighted model corrects an intuitively wrong unweighted ranking (GPT-4 dropping to 3rd) and achieves higher Spearman correlation with human-preference-based BTL rankings (0.9955 vs 0.9699).

Multiple robustness checks are included (tie-handling ablation, sparse/connected comparison-graph subsampling, a length-covariate extension of the judge discrimination parameter), which strengthens confidence that the core findings are not artifacts of specific design choices.

The paper provides a practical, well-documented optimization algorithm (projected Adam with explicit gradient formulas) and reports data efficiency gains (narrower CIs, higher correlation to reference scores) that are plausible and consistent with the theory.
Clear discussion of limitations (global scalar discrimination parameter, conditional independence assumption, sparse/imbalanced designs) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution—multiplying a judge-specific scalar discrimination parameter into a BTL log-odds, akin to a 2-parameter IRT model—is conceptually close to prior IRT-based pairwise aggregation (Otani et al., 2016); the delta (reference-free, fully randomized design, asymptotic theory) is real but incremental rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

No direct empirical comparison against the explicitly discussed competing methods REM and GTR/FTR, despite these being positioned as the main prior art for LLM ranking without ground truth; only the unweighted BTL baseline is compared throughout, which is the easiest baseline to beat and does not establish superiority over existing heuristic weighting schemes.

The validation that gamma correctly identifies 'high-quality' vs 'low-quality' judges (Section 5.4) relies on informal, subjective a priori labeling by the authors rather than an independent, rigorous ground-truth measure of judge quality (e.g., correlation with large-scale human annotations per judge), weakening the causal claim that gamma captures 'true' reliability rather than some other artifact (e.g., verbosity, confidence calibration, or self-similarity to the aggregated ranking it is fit against).

The model assumes conditionally independent judge errors and a single global (or, in the appendix extension, length-covariate) discrimination parameter per judge; this ignores well-documented judge-specific biases in LLM-as-judge settings (self-preference/self-enhancement bias, position bias, verbosity bias), which are arguably more consequential confounds than generic 'noise' and are not modeled or empirically probed despite being highly relevant to the framework's real-world reliability.

The magnitude of the reported efficiency gains (e.g., 5.4%–13.5% CI-width reduction) is fairly modest, and it is unclear whether this translates into materially different practical leaderboard decisions beyond the illustrative GPT-4 ranking anomaly.

The central motivating claim that 'more data can make evaluation more confidently wrong' is demonstrated only under a simulation explicitly constructed so the unweighted model is misspecified relative to the true data-generating process—an expected consequence of model misspecification rather than a surprising empirical finding about real judge panels.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of a judge-aware extension of the BTL model, including a full identifiability proof (Theorem 3.2/Corollary 3.3) and consistency/asymptotic normality results (Theorem 3.4) with detailed, careful proofs in the appendix, which is uncommon in LLM-evaluation papers and enables principled Wald confidence intervals.

The empirical study is broad in scope, covering simulations (convergence rate, coverage/width of CIs), three public benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback), and a newly collected 45-model/18-judge in-house dataset, plus several robustness checks (tie handling, sparse comparison graphs, a length-covariate extension of the discrimination parameter).

The core motivating observation -- that pooling judges of heterogeneous reliability under a misspecified homogeneous-judge BTL model yields confidence intervals that shrink around a biased point estimate as more data arrive -- is a clear and practically important point, and the simulation in Section 4.2 illustrates it cleanly.

The method is computationally simple (a projected-Adam MLE with an explicit, cheap gradient), and the algorithm and simulation settings are specified in enough detail (Appendices B, C) to support reproducibility of the synthetic experiments.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the proposed γ_k multiplicative discrimination parameter is essentially the 2-parameter IRT/Thurstonian discrimination model already used by Otani et al. (2016) for crowdsourced pairwise MT evaluation; the paper's claimed distinction (reference-free vs. fixed-reference design) is a relatively small extension rather than a new modeling idea, and the asymptotic theory, while rigorous, is a fairly standard M-estimation argument applied to this model.

Several key empirical validations are circular or self-referential: in Section 5.3 and 5.4 the 'ground truth' used to judge the weighted model's efficiency/accuracy is itself produced by the full-data weighted model (e.g., 'reference scores are obtained by fitting the judge-aware weighted model on the complete available comparison dataset'); comparing the weighted model to a weighted reference and the unweighted model to an unweighted reference does not demonstrate that the weighted model's rankings are actually closer to any independent truth, only that each model is self-consistent as data accumulate.

No empirical comparison is made against the heuristic baselines discussed at length in Related Work (REM, GTR/FTR, Crowd-BT, Product-of-Experts), despite these being the most directly comparable existing methods for ranking LLMs without ground truth; without such comparisons, the claimed practical advantage of the judge-aware approach over 'existing approaches' is not substantiated.

The model assumes judge errors are purely a matter of discrimination/noise scale (γ_k), with no provision for systematic bias (e.g., self-preference, verbosity/position bias, or consistent miscalibration toward certain response styles) -- a well-documented property of LLM judges. This is a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption for the stated application, and the paper does not empirically or theoretically assess robustness to such bias, despite it being arguably the dominant source of judge unreliability in practice.

The 'high-quality' vs. 'low-quality' judge labels in Section 5.4 are said to be 'manually identified... a priori' with no description of the criteria or procedure used, undermining reproducibility and raising concern about selection effects that could favor the proposed method.

Validation against established rankings is based on very small, under-powered comparisons (5 models in Table 1, qualitative description of rank order preservation in Table 3) rather than systematic statistical tests of improved agreement with human preference, limiting the strength of the significance claims.

The treatment of ties (y=0.5) and the choice of filtering/anonymized prompt templates, while discussed, are ad hoc design choices whose influence on the headline comparisons (e.g., Spearman ρ with human BTL rankings) is only checked in a limited robustness appendix rather than built into the main analysis.

strengths: The core model is a clean, well-motivated extension of the Bradley-Terry-Luce model that introduces a single judge-specific discrimination parameter, directly addressing a real and under-modeled issue (judge heterogeneity) in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines.

Strong theoretical contribution: the paper proves identifiability up to natural normalization (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3) and establishes consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE (Theorem 3.4) with full, carefully written proofs in the appendix, including explicit Fisher information invertibility arguments under the random design.

Simulation studies convincingly validate the asymptotic theory: estimated convergence rates are close to the predicted O(1/T), and the judge-aware model achieves near-nominal coverage while the unweighted BTL model shows coverage degradation that worsens with more data, nicely illustrating the paper's 'confidently wrong' motivating claim.

Diverse empirical validation across four datasets (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a newly collected 45-model/18-judge in-house dataset), including correlation with human-preference rankings (Chatbot Arena Spearman ρ=0.9955 vs 0.9699) and plausible recovery of manually identified high/low-quality judges.

Thorough appendix with multiple robustness analyses: tie-handling sensitivity, sparse/disconnected comparison graphs, and a length-covariate extension of the discrimination parameter with its own identifiability proof, showing the authors stress-tested their own assumptions.
Reasonably clear writing and good positioning relative to related statistical ranking literature (BTL extensions, Crowd-BT, IRT-based aggregation, REM/GTR/FTR).
weaknesses: Despite extensively discussing REM, GTR/FTR, and Product-of-Experts aggregation as competing heuristic-weighting approaches in related work, the empirical section only compares against the unweighted BTL baseline; no direct quantitative comparison against these alternative judge-weighting schemes is provided, weakening the significance claim that the proposed method is preferable to existing heuristics.

The practical efficiency gains on real data are fairly modest (e.g., 13.5% and 5.4% reduction in average CI width), which is a less compelling demonstration of practical importance than the dramatic effects shown in the idealized simulations; the gap between simulated and real-world gains is not discussed.

Validation against 'ground truth' in the heterogeneous-judge experiment and in the model-size vs. discrimination analysis relies on soft, manually labeled notions of judge quality or on correlation with other possibly noisy benchmarks (MT-Bench scores, UltraFeedback ratings), so claims of 'recovering' judge quality or model quality are only indirectly validated rather than rigorously verified against independent ground truth.

The model's core assumption of conditionally independent judge errors given latent scores is acknowledged as a limitation but not tested empirically; judges drawn from the same model family (as used in the in-house panel) plausibly exhibit correlated errors that could bias the reliability-weighting scheme in ways not explored.

Some practical fragility is evident but underexplored: one judge had to be excluded from the in-house analysis due to γ̂≈0 causing numerical instability, suggesting the method may be sensitive to near-degenerate discrimination estimates in finite samples, which is not deeply analyzed.

The real-data subsampling and heterogeneity experiments use a small number of replicates (e.g., five repeats), with relatively limited reporting of variability/confidence in the reported correlation improvements themselves.
